div.head: Section 406
div.p: SOCRATES. Someone was relating to us just now concerning Cleitophon the son of Aristonymus, that conversing with Lysias he was blaming the pastimes with Socrates, and exceedingly praising the association with Thrasymachus.

CLEITOPHON. Whoever he was, Socrates, did not remember correctly to you the arguments I made about you to Lysias; for in some things indeed I was not praising you, but in some things I was also praising you. But since it is clear you are blaming me, though pretending to care nothing, I would most gladly relate them to you myself, since we also happen to be alone, so that you may consider me less to be in a bad state towards you. For now perhaps you have not heard correctly, so that you appear to be more harshly disposed towards me than is necessary; but if you give me freedom of speech, I would receive it most gladly and wish to speak.

div.head: Section 407
div.p: SOCRATES. But indeed it would be shameful for me not to endure when you are eager to help; for it is clear that recognizing in what way I am worse and better, I shall practice and pursue some things, and flee others with all my might.

CLEITOPHON. You shall hear. For I, Socrates, associating with you was often astounded hearing you, and it seemed to me you spoke most beautifully beside other men, whenever rebuking men, like a god upon a tragic machine, you sang saying: Whither are you carried, men? And are you ignorant doing nothing of what is necessary, you who concerning money have all zeal how it shall be yours, but concerning your sons to whom you will hand these things down how they shall know to use these things justly, you neither find teachers for them of justice, if indeed it can be taught—and if it must be practiced and trained, those who will sufficiently train and make them practice—nor indeed even before did you thus care for yourselves. But seeing that you yourselves and your children have sufficiently learned letters and music and gymnastics—which indeed you consider to be a complete education of virtue—and then nevertheless become bad concerning money, how do you not despise the present education nor seek those who will stop you from this lack of music? And yet it is because of this disharmony and laziness, but not because of a lack of measure in the foot against the lyre, that both brother to brother and cities to cities, acting without measure and harmoniously towards one another, factionalize and warring do and suffer the utmost things. But you say that the unjust are unjust not through lack of education nor through ignorance but willingly, and then again you dare to say that injustice is shameful and hated by the gods; how then indeed could anyone willingly choose such an evil? Whoever is weaker, you say, than pleasures. Therefore is this also involuntary, if indeed conquering is voluntary? So that from every way the argument takes injustice to be involuntary, and that every man privately and all cities publicly together must make more care than now. Therefore, Socrates, whenever I hear you often saying these things, I very much admire and wonderfully praise them. And whenever again you say what follows this, that those who practice their bodies, but have neglected their soul do another such thing, neglecting the ruling part, but having been zealous concerning the part to be ruled. And whenever you say that whatever someone does not know how to use, it is better to leave the use of this; if indeed someone does not know how to use eyes nor ears nor the whole body, for this one neither to hear nor to see nor to use any other use of the body is better than to use it in any way.

div.head: Section 408
div.p: CLEITOPHON. And indeed concerning art it is in the same way; for whoever indeed does not know how to use his own lyre, it is clear that he does not know how to use his neighbor's either, nor whoever not the others', nor his own, nor any other of instruments nor of possessions. And indeed this argument ends beautifully for you, that whoever does not know how to use a soul, for him to keep his soul quiet and not to live is better than to live acting by himself; but if there should be some necessity to live, it is better for such a man to pass his life as a slave than as a free man, just as handing over the rudders of thought to another in a ship, to the one having learned the piloting of men, which indeed you, Socrates, often name statesmanship, saying this same thing is both judging and justice. To these arguments and very many others like them and very beautifully spoken, that virtue can be taught and one must most of all care for oneself, I have almost never spoken against them nor do I think I ever shall speak against them later, and I consider them most protreptic and most helpful, and literally as if waking us up sleeping. I indeed applied my mind as going to hear what comes after these things, questioning not you at first, Socrates, but those of your age and fellow-desirers or comrades, or however one must name such things in relation to you. For questioning first those of these thought to be most something by you, inquiring what would be the argument after these things, and stretching it out to them in a way according to you, Best men, I said, how on earth do we now accept Socrates' exhortation of us toward virtue? As this being the only thing, but it is not in the matter to go through it and grasp it completely, but this will be a work for us throughout our whole life, to exhort those not yet exhorted, and they again others? Or must we question Socrates and each other what is after this, having agreed this itself is to be done by a man, what is from here? How do we say one must begin concerning the learning of justice? Just as if someone exhorted us to make care of the body, seeing us taking no forethought like children that there is some gymnastics and medicine, and then reproached us, saying that it is shameful to make all care of wheat and barley and vines, and as many things as we labor through and acquire for the sake of the body, but of this itself to discover no art nor machine, how the body shall be as good as possible, and these things being so.

div.head: Section 409
div.p: CLEITOPHON. But if we questioned the one exhorting us to these things: And what do you say these arts are? He would perhaps say that it is gymnastics and medicine. And now indeed what do we say the art upon the virtue of the soul is? Let it be said. He who seemed to be the most robust of them answering to these things said to me that this art is the very one you hear Socrates saying, he said, no other than justice. But when I said Do not tell me only the name, but thus. Medicine is said to be some art; and its results are twofold, the one to always produce other doctors besides those that are, and the other health; and of these the latter is no longer an art, but the work of the art teaching and being taught, which indeed we call health. And of carpentry in the same way a house and carpentry are the one a work, and the other a teaching. Let it be in the same way for justice that the one is to make just men, just as there each makes craftsmen; but the other, what is the work that the just man can do for us, what do we say this is? Tell me. This one, as I think, answered the advantageous, but another the necessary, another the helpful, and another the profitable. I indeed returned saying that Also there these names are in each of the arts, to do correctly, profitable things, helpful things and the other such things; but toward what all these things tend, each art will say its own thing, such as carpentry the well, the beautifully, the necessarily, so that the wooden vessels, it will say, are produced, which indeed are not an art. Let it be said indeed also of justice in the same way. Finally one of your comrades answered me, Socrates, who indeed seemed to speak most elegantly, that this is the peculiar work of justice, which belongs to none of the others, to make friendship in the cities. But this one again being questioned said that friendship is a good thing and never bad, but he did not accept the friendships of children and those of beasts, which we name with this name, to be friendships when questioned; for it happened to him that the majority of such were more harmful than good. Fleeing indeed such a thing he said that such are not even friendships, but those naming them thus name them falsely; and that the being and truly friendship is most clearly agreement. And being questioned about agreement whether he meant it to be a sameness of opinion or knowledge, he dishonored sameness of opinion; for many and harmful samenesses of opinion of men were forced to arise, but he had agreed that friendship is altogether good and a work of justice, so that he said agreement was the same thing and being knowledge, but not opinion.

div.head: Section 410
div.p:
CLEITOPHON. When indeed we were here in the argument being at a loss,
those present were sufficient to rebuke him and to say that the argument had run around into the same thing as the first things, and they said that Also medicine is a certain agreement and all the arts, and they are able to say concerning what they are; but the justice or agreement called by you, where it is tending, has escaped, and what on earth its work is is unclear. Finally, Socrates, I was asking you yourself these things, and you told me that it belongs to justice to harm enemies, but to do well to friends. But later it appeared that the just man never harms anyone; for he does all things for the benefit of all. I have endured these things not once nor twice but for a long time and persevering I have given up, considering that you do most beautifully of men in exhorting to the care of virtue, but of two things one, either you are able only this much, but nothing further, which would happen also concerning any other art whatsoever, such as someone not being a pilot practicing the praise concerning it, how much it is worth to men, and concerning the other arts in the same way; someone might perhaps bring this same thing against you also concerning justice, that you are not more a knower of justice, because you beautifully praise it. Yet my own opinion is not thus; but of two things one, either you do not know or you do not wish to share it with me. Because of these things indeed I think I will proceed also to Thrasymachus and elsewhere wherever I can, being at a loss; since if indeed you are willing to cease from these exhorting arguments toward me now, but as, if I had been exhorted concerning gymnastics that one must not neglect the body, you would say what follows the exhorting argument such as what sort of care my body being by nature requires, let this same thing happen also now. Put Cleitophon agreeing that it is ridiculous to make care of other things, but of the soul, for the sake of which we labor through the other things, to have neglected this; and think that I have now said all the other things thus which are next to these, which also just now I went through. And begging you I say to do in no other way, so that I may not, just as now, praise you in some things to Lysias and to the others, but in some things also blame you. For I will say, Socrates, that to a man not yet exhorted you are worth everything, but to one exhorted almost even an impediment to becoming happy having come to the end of virtue.
